newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu chides Egypt on peace pressure.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu chides Egypt on peace pressure.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, turning aside Arab charges of Israeli foot-dragging on Middle East peace, chided Egypt on Sunday for tying a planned regional economic summit to further moves by the Jewish state.

Egypt, a key mediator in five years of Arab-Israeli talks, has said there must be tangible progress towards peace if it is to go ahead with organising the conference set for Cairo in November. The meeting is meant to integrate Israel into the regional economy.

"To threaten us, as pressure on us, to cancel the Cairo conference, is like a man who cuts off his nose to spite his face. We are not seriously listening to these things," Netanyahu told Israel Radio in an interview marking the Jewish New Year.
Netanyahu said he doubted Egypt would suspend the conference, saying the meeting was in Cairo's own interest.
If Egypt "doesn't want to hold the economic conference, let it not seek political excuses," he said. "I do not advise anyone to use tools like this against us. It will also be of no help."

In Cairo, diplomats said three months of inaction by Netanyahu had prompted his Arab neighbours to consider a more robust approach towards peace negotiations, including such steps as a boycott on multilateral talks with the Jewish state.

Syria and its ally Lebanon have been boycotting the multilateral talks on regional cooperation for years but countries like Egypt and Jordan have argued in the past that such talks help to convince Israel of their good intentions.

Following his upset May election victory over Shimon Peres, Netanyahu alarmed the Arab world by rejecting the principle of trading occupied Arab land for peace, the foundation of previously held U.S.-sponsored talks.

Egypt in 1979 became the first Arab country to sign a formal peace treaty with Israel. Then-prime minister Menachem Begin, a founder of Netanyahu's Likud, departed from the party's hardline ideology to approve the pact, which led to a full pullout from all Egyptian land taken by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.
Israeli media have said Netanyahu's defence establishment has debated the significance of large-scale Egyptian army exercises held in recent days.
"We must stand determined here, follow with caution any movement of forces," Netanyahu said, referring to the Egyptian exercises and to recent reports of Syrian troop movements.

"We are certainly not sitting back carefree regarding certain possibilities, but we are also making it clear to the other side that our direction is that of peace -- meaning that there must be mutual compromise and not one-sided surrender by Israel to the demands of the Arabs, which is what we had with the previous (Peres) government," Netanyahu said.

On his relations with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, Netanyahu acknowledged he had written in a book published earlier this year: "Yasser Arafat contributed more than anyone else to the spread of international terrorism."
Israeli hawks have criticised the Israeli leader for meeting Arafat this month. Doves criticised Netanyahu for waiting so long.

Netanyahu said that although Arafat's forces had ceased guerrilla operations since the 1993 Israel-PLO peace deal and had cracked down on Islamic groups that killed scores of Israelis in suicide attacks, he had put Arafat on notice "that we will tolerate no return to the prior situation".
Arafat aide Marwan Kanafani said: "Netanyahu must stop his threatening statements against the Palestinian Authority and his Arab neighbours if he wants to pursue the peace process."
